What China's 600 GWh Battery Surge Reveals About Global Energy Infrastructure

The transformation of global energy markets is accelerating at unprecedented speeds, driven by the convergence of artificial intelligence computing demands, renewable energy deployment, and grid modernisation requirements. China battery production expansion has emerged as the critical bottleneck determining which economies can successfully transition to sustainable energy systems while supporting next-generation computing infrastructure.

China's battery production landscape is experiencing a dramatic reconfiguration that extends far beyond traditional electric vehicle applications. The strategic pivot toward energy storage systems reflects fundamental changes in how nations approach energy security, grid stability, and technological competitiveness in an increasingly digital economy.

What Does China's 600 GWh Battery Expansion Mean for Global Energy Markets?

China battery production expansion has committed to adding over 600 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of new energy storage system production capacity within just the first two months of 2026. This expansion represents a fundamental shift in global energy infrastructure development, with implications extending far beyond traditional battery applications.

Breaking Down the Scale of China's 2026 Manufacturing Commitments

The scope of China battery production expansion demonstrates unprecedented industrial coordination. Nineteen mainland Chinese battery producers are collectively investing 180 billion yuan ($26.3 billion) to construct new lithium-ion battery manufacturing facilities. When completed, these projects will generate 900 GWh of annual production capacity, with some facilities scheduled to begin operations in late 2026.

To contextualise this scale, each gigawatt-hour of battery capacity can supply approximately 750,000 households for an entire year. The planned 900 GWh annual capacity theoretically represents enough energy storage to power 675 million households globally, highlighting the massive infrastructure implications of China's expansion plans.

Energy Storage Systems vs Electric Vehicle Battery Allocation Strategy

The strategic allocation of new capacity reveals critical insights into global energy market evolution. Seventy percent of the 900 GWh capacity will be dedicated to energy storage systems, while only thirty percent will serve electric vehicle applications. This 70/30 split represents a dramatic departure from previous battery manufacturing priorities.

Energy storage systems comprise integrated solutions including:

Battery cells and modules

Battery management systems for operational control

Power conversion equipment for grid integration

Control systems managing energy flow and storage

Investment Capital Flow Analysis: $26.3 Billion in New Facility Development

The $26.3 billion investment across 19 manufacturers represents an average commitment of approximately $1.38 billion per company. This capital deployment indicates sustained confidence in energy storage market growth, with manufacturers expecting returns on investments spanning multiple years of production cycles.

The investment timeline suggests manufacturers anticipate continued growth in artificial intelligence computing infrastructure, which requires massive electrical power paired with renewable energy sources. Energy storage systems bridge the gap between intermittent renewable generation and consistent power demands from data centres and computing facilities.

How Will China's Battery Capacity Compare to Global Competitors by 2027?

China's 600+ GWh capacity announcement represents approximately 10.3 times the total battery storage capacity installed across the United States during 2025, which totalled 58 GWh. This comparison underscores the widening gap between Chinese production capabilities and international competitors.

US Market Position: The 58 GWh Baseline Challenge

The United States deployed 58 GWh of battery storage capacity in 2025, establishing a baseline for measuring China's expansion scale. However, this figure represents installed storage capacity rather than annual production capacity, creating methodological differences in direct comparisons.

American battery manufacturing focuses primarily on domestic market needs, with companies like Tesla, GM, and Ford developing integrated supply chains. The US approach emphasises technological innovation and domestic supply chain security rather than absolute production volume.

European Battery Alliance Response Strategies

European manufacturers are pursuing technological differentiation through solid-state battery development and advanced materials research. The European Battery Alliance coordinates industrial policy across member states, emphasising sustainable production methods and circular economy principles.

European capacity expansion focuses on strategic partnerships with automotive manufacturers and grid operators, prioritising quality and technological advancement over pure production volume. This approach creates opportunities for premium market positioning despite lower absolute capacity numbers.

South Korea and Japan's Competitive Positioning

South Korean manufacturers like LG Energy Solution and SK Innovation maintain technological leadership in specific battery chemistries and applications. Japanese companies including Panasonic focus on high-performance applications and advanced materials development.

These manufacturers compete through technological innovation rather than capacity scaling, developing specialised applications for aerospace, medical devices, and premium automotive segments where performance requirements exceed standard specifications.

Which Chinese Battery Manufacturers Are Leading the Expansion Wave?

The expansion involves major established players alongside emerging manufacturers seeking market share through aggressive capacity additions. Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd (CATL) leads as China's dominant battery manufacturer, while Gotion High-tech represents emerging companies challenging established market positions.

CATL's Market Dominance Strategy and Production Scaling

CATL maintains its position as China's leading battery manufacturer through continuous capacity expansion and technological development. The company's strategy involves vertical integration across the battery supply chain, from raw materials processing through finished battery systems.

Furthermore, CATL's expansion focuses on both domestic Chinese markets and international operations, establishing manufacturing facilities in Europe and considering North American production. This geographic diversification strategy reduces geopolitical risks while maintaining cost advantages.

BYD's Integrated Manufacturing Approach

BYD operates as both a battery manufacturer and electric vehicle producer, creating synergies between battery development and automotive applications. This integrated approach allows BYD to optimise battery specifications for specific vehicle platforms while developing energy storage solutions.

The company's blade battery technology emphasises safety and longevity, positioning BYD for applications requiring extended operational life and minimal maintenance. These characteristics align with utility-scale energy storage requirements.

Emerging Players: Gotion High-tech and Market Disruption Potential

Gotion High-tech represents the emerging manufacturer category, pursuing aggressive expansion strategies to capture market share from established competitors. These companies often focus on cost optimisation and rapid scaling rather than premium applications.

Emerging manufacturers create competitive pressure on established players, driving innovation and cost reduction across the industry. Their participation in the 600+ GWh expansion indicates confidence in sustained market growth and willingness to invest in production capacity ahead of confirmed demand.

Why Are Energy Storage Systems Driving 70% of New Battery Production?

The strategic focus on energy storage systems reflects fundamental changes in global energy infrastructure requirements. Artificial intelligence computing infrastructure generates massive electricity demands while renewable energy adoption accelerates globally, creating unprecedented needs for grid-scale energy storage.

AI Computing Infrastructure Demands and Grid Stability Requirements

Modern artificial intelligence applications require enormous computational power, with large data centres consuming electricity equivalent to small cities. A typical large-scale AI computing facility can draw 100-300+ megawatts continuously, creating substantial challenges for grid operators managing power supply.

These facilities increasingly operate on renewable energy to meet sustainability commitments, but solar and wind generation patterns don't align with consistent computing demands. Energy storage systems provide the critical buffer allowing renewable energy sources to power AI infrastructure reliably.

The relationship between AI development and energy storage creates compound growth opportunities. As AI applications expand across industries, the associated energy storage requirements multiply, driving sustained demand for battery-grade lithium refinery capacity.

Renewable Energy Integration Challenges Across Global Markets

Renewable energy sources present inherent intermittency challenges that energy storage systems address. Solar generation peaks during midday hours while wind patterns vary unpredictably, creating mismatches with electrical demand patterns.

Energy Storage System Applications by Sector:

Application Type Primary Function Typical Capacity Range Utility-scale renewable integration Grid balancing and peak shaving 50-500 MWh Commercial backup power systems Business continuity during outages 1-50 MWh Residential energy independence Household backup and solar storage 10-100 kWh Industrial load balancing Manufacturing process stability 5-200 MWh

Grid operators worldwide are implementing energy storage requirements for new renewable energy projects, creating regulatory demand for battery systems. These mandates ensure renewable energy installations contribute to grid stability rather than creating additional volatility.

Grid Modernisation Trends in Developing Economies

Developing economies often lack extensive electrical grid infrastructure, creating opportunities for modern grid designs incorporating energy storage from initial deployment. These markets can implement advanced grid management systems without retrofitting existing infrastructure.

Countries in Africa, Southeast Asia, and Latin America are developing renewable energy projects with integrated storage systems, bypassing traditional fossil fuel infrastructure. This leapfrog development pattern creates substantial markets for energy storage systems manufactured as part of the critical minerals energy transition.

One gigawatt-hour of battery capacity can power approximately 750,000 households for an entire year, highlighting the massive scale of China's planned expansion and its potential impact on global energy access.

What Are the Economic Implications of China's Battery Manufacturing Dominance?

China battery production expansion creates significant economic implications through supply chain control, pricing power, and international trade dynamics. The scale of investment and production capacity positions Chinese manufacturers to influence global battery markets substantially.

Supply Chain Control and Pricing Power Dynamics

Chinese manufacturers' capacity expansion creates potential supply chain concentration risks for global energy storage deployment. With 900 GWh of annual production capacity, Chinese companies could supply the majority of global energy storage requirements, creating dependencies for international projects.

This concentration provides Chinese manufacturers with significant pricing power, particularly for standardised energy storage applications where technological differentiation is limited. Large-scale production enables cost advantages that smaller international competitors struggle to match.

The economic leverage extends beyond battery cells to include critical materials processing, battery management systems, and power electronics manufacturing. Chinese companies increasingly control multiple supply chain stages, amplifying their market influence.

Technology Transfer and Intellectual Property Considerations

International customers purchasing Chinese battery systems gain access to current technology while potentially becoming dependent on continued technology updates and support services. This relationship creates ongoing economic ties extending beyond initial equipment purchases.

Intellectual property concerns arise when Chinese manufacturers develop technologies through partnerships with international companies, then scale these technologies through massive domestic production capacity. The balance between collaboration and competition creates complex economic relationships.

Trade Policy Responses from Western Governments

Western governments are implementing various policy responses to address Chinese battery manufacturing dominance, including domestic production incentives, import restrictions, and strategic partnership requirements. These policies aim to maintain supply chain security while managing economic competitiveness.

The United States and European Union are developing domestic battery manufacturing capabilities through subsidies, tax incentives, and regulatory preferences for locally-produced systems. However, the scale of Chinese capacity expansion presents significant challenges for these policy approaches.

How Will Overcapacity Concerns Shape China's Battery Export Strategy?

The massive scale of China's planned battery production capacity raises questions about market absorption and potential overcapacity scenarios. With 900 GWh of annual production capacity, Chinese manufacturers must develop export strategies to utilise their full production potential.

Domestic Market Saturation and International Expansion Plans

China's domestic market for energy storage systems is expanding rapidly but may not absorb the full 900 GWh annual production capacity. This creates incentives for Chinese manufacturers to develop international markets and establish global distribution networks.

Export strategies likely focus on developing economies with expanding renewable energy infrastructure and limited domestic battery manufacturing capabilities. These markets offer growth opportunities without direct competition from established local manufacturers.

Chinese manufacturers may also pursue strategic partnerships with international project developers, offering competitive pricing and integrated solutions for utility-scale energy storage projects. These partnerships provide market access while reducing regulatory barriers in target countries.

Quality Standards vs Volume Production Trade-offs

Rapid capacity expansion creates potential tensions between production volume and quality standards. Maintaining consistent quality across multiple new manufacturing facilities requires substantial investment in process control, testing equipment, and workforce training.

International markets often require compliance with specific quality standards and certification processes that may differ from domestic Chinese requirements. Managing these compliance requirements while scaling production presents operational challenges for manufacturers.

Quality concerns could create market segmentation opportunities, with premium applications requiring higher standards commanding price premiums while cost-sensitive applications accept standardised quality levels.

Government Regulatory Adjustments and Industry Consolidation

Chinese government policies may evolve to address potential overcapacity through industry consolidation, export promotion, or production coordination among manufacturers. Regulatory adjustments could influence how the 900 GWh capacity is utilised across domestic and international markets.

Industry consolidation could occur naturally as smaller manufacturers struggle with competitive pressures from large-scale producers. This consolidation process creates both risks and opportunities for investors depending on their portfolio positioning.

What Technologies Are Driving Next-Generation Battery Performance?

Technological developments in battery chemistry, energy density, and manufacturing processes are enabling the massive capacity expansion while improving performance characteristics. These advances make energy storage systems more economically viable for diverse applications.

Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) Dominance in Cost-Effective Applications

Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) battery chemistry has emerged as the preferred technology for many energy storage applications due to its cost advantages, safety characteristics, and long cycle life. Chinese manufacturers have achieved significant cost reductions in LFP production, making these batteries competitive with alternative technologies.

LFP batteries offer 3,000-5,000 charge cycles compared to 1,000-2,000 cycles for traditional lithium-ion chemistries. This longevity makes LFP particularly attractive for utility-scale energy storage where replacement costs are significant operational considerations.

The safety characteristics of LFP technology reduce fire risks and thermal runaway concerns, enabling simplified installation procedures and reduced insurance costs for energy storage projects. These advantages contribute to lower total system costs beyond the battery components themselves.

Solid-State Battery Breakthroughs and Commercial Viability Timelines

Solid-state battery technology represents the next major advancement in battery performance, offering higher energy density and improved safety characteristics. Chinese manufacturers are investing in solid-state development while maintaining focus on current lithium-ion production scaling.

Commercial solid-state batteries are expected to achieve 400-800+ Wh/kg energy density compared to 250-300 Wh/kg for current lithium-ion technologies. These improvements enable smaller, lighter battery systems for equivalent energy storage capacity.

However, solid-state manufacturing costs remain significantly higher than lithium-ion production, limiting initial applications to premium markets. Mass production cost reductions may require several years of development and manufacturing optimisation.

Energy Density Improvements: From 250 Wh/kg to 800+ Wh/kg Potential

Current lithium-ion batteries achieve approximately 250-300 Wh/kg energy density in commercial applications, while laboratory developments demonstrate potential for 400-500 Wh/kg in near-term improvements. Advanced solid-state technologies target 800+ Wh/kg energy density in future generations.

These energy density improvements enable more compact energy storage installations, reducing real estate requirements and installation costs for utility-scale projects. Higher density also improves transportation economics for mobile applications.

Manufacturing scale advantages allow Chinese producers to implement energy density improvements across large production volumes, accelerating the transition from laboratory developments to commercial applications. The focus on these improvements reflects understanding that decarbonisation mining benefits require enhanced technology performance.

Which Global Regions Will Benefit Most from China's Battery Production Surge?

China's expanded battery production capacity will create supply availability for global energy storage projects, with certain regions positioned to benefit disproportionately based on infrastructure development needs and economic conditions.

Southeast Asian Infrastructure Development Projects

Southeast Asian countries are implementing large-scale renewable energy projects requiring substantial energy storage capacity. Countries like Indonesia, Thailand, and Vietnam have announced utility-scale solar and wind projects that depend on battery storage for grid integration.

These markets offer favourable conditions for Chinese battery manufacturers, including geographic proximity, established trade relationships, and regulatory environments open to international technology suppliers. Infrastructure development timelines align with Chinese production capacity availability.

Regional economic development initiatives, including China's Belt and Road Initiative, create financing mechanisms supporting energy storage project development in Southeast Asian markets. These financing arrangements often favour Chinese technology suppliers.

African Renewable Energy Initiative Support

African countries are developing renewable energy capacity to address growing electricity demand and improve energy access. Many African nations lack extensive existing electrical infrastructure, creating opportunities for modern grid designs incorporating energy storage from initial development.

The African continent's abundant solar and wind resources require energy storage systems to maximise utilisation and provide reliable power supply. Chinese battery manufacturers can supply cost-effective storage solutions supporting these renewable energy developments.

International development organisations and climate finance mechanisms provide funding for African renewable energy projects, creating market opportunities for competitively-priced energy storage systems from Chinese manufacturers.

Latin American Grid Modernisation Opportunities

Latin American countries are modernising electrical grids and expanding renewable energy capacity, creating demand for advanced energy storage systems. Countries like Chile, Brazil, and Mexico have established renewable energy targets requiring storage integration.

Mining operations throughout Latin America are adopting renewable energy systems with battery storage to reduce operational costs and environmental impacts. These industrial applications provide stable, large-scale demand for energy storage systems.

Regional trade agreements and economic partnerships facilitate technology imports from China, creating favourable conditions for battery system exports to Latin American markets.

How Should Investors Evaluate China's Battery Sector Growth Trajectory?

Investment analysis of China's battery sector expansion requires careful consideration of multiple risk factors, market dynamics, and long-term sustainability indicators. The scale of capacity addition creates both opportunities and potential concerns for investors.

Market Concentration Risks and Diversification Strategies

The concentration of battery manufacturing capacity among Chinese producers creates market concentration risks for global energy storage supply chains. Investors should evaluate exposure to supply chain disruptions, regulatory changes, and geopolitical tensions affecting Chinese manufacturers.

Diversification strategies might include investments in non-Chinese battery manufacturers, battery materials suppliers, or energy storage system integrators that can utilise batteries from multiple sources. This approach reduces dependency on any single manufacturing region.

Investment Risk Assessment Matrix:

Risk Category Impact Level Mitigation Strategies Technology obsolescence risk High Diversified technology investments Geopolitical trade restrictions Medium Geographic diversification Raw material price volatility High Vertical integration or long-term contracts Market oversaturation potential Medium Focus on growth markets and applications

Raw Material Supply Chain Dependencies

Battery manufacturing requires critical materials including lithium, cobalt, nickel, and rare earth elements. China's battery expansion increases demand for these materials, potentially creating price pressures and supply chain constraints.

Investors should evaluate raw material supply security, price volatility risks, and potential substitution technologies that could affect material demand. Recycling technology development may also influence long-term material requirements and supply dynamics.

Geographic concentration of critical material deposits creates additional supply chain risks, particularly for cobalt (concentrated in Democratic Republic of Congo) and lithium (concentrated in South America and Australia). Understanding lithium market supply-demand dynamics becomes crucial for investment decisions.

Long-term Sustainability of Current Expansion Rates

The current pace of battery manufacturing expansion may not be sustainable indefinitely, as market demand must eventually align with production capacity. Investors should evaluate demand growth scenarios and potential capacity utilisation rates.

Market maturation could lead to industry consolidation, with less efficient manufacturers exiting the market or being acquired by larger competitors. This consolidation process creates both risks and opportunities for investors depending on their portfolio positioning.

Technological disruptions, such as alternative energy storage technologies or breakthrough battery improvements, could affect the long-term value of current manufacturing investments.

What Are the Environmental and Sustainability Implications?

China's massive battery production expansion carries significant environmental implications through manufacturing processes, resource consumption, and end-of-life disposal considerations. These factors influence the overall sustainability of the energy storage transition.

Battery manufacturing processes are energy-intensive, particularly for lithium-ion cell production and materials processing. The carbon footprint of producing 900 GWh annually could be substantial unless manufacturing facilities utilise renewable energy sources.

Chinese manufacturers are increasingly implementing renewable energy systems at production facilities to reduce manufacturing carbon footprints. However, the rapid expansion timeline may create pressures to utilise available energy sources regardless of carbon intensity.

Life-cycle analysis must consider both manufacturing emissions and operational benefits from enabling renewable energy storage. The net carbon impact depends on how manufactured batteries are ultimately utilised and what energy sources they replace or enable.

Battery Recycling Infrastructure Development Needs

The massive scale of battery production will eventually require corresponding recycling capacity to manage end-of-life battery systems. Current recycling infrastructure may be inadequate for processing 900 GWh worth of batteries annually when they reach end-of-life.

Recycling technology development focuses on recovering valuable materials including lithium, cobalt, nickel, and other components for reuse in new battery production. Effective recycling reduces dependence on virgin material mining while managing waste disposal challenges.

Regulatory frameworks for battery recycling are evolving globally, with some jurisdictions implementing producer responsibility requirements that hold manufacturers accountable for end-of-life battery management.

Resource Extraction Impact on Global Lithium Markets

Increased battery production drives demand for lithium, potentially accelerating mining operations in Australia, Chile, Argentina, and other lithium-rich regions. The environmental impacts of lithium extraction vary significantly depending on extraction methods and local environmental conditions.

Brine extraction methods used in South American salt flats require large water volumes and extended processing times, potentially affecting local water resources. Hard rock mining operations in Australia and other regions have different environmental considerations including land disturbance and processing waste.

Alternative lithium sources, including recycled batteries and alternative extraction technologies, may help mitigate environmental impacts while supporting continued battery production growth.

What Are the Key Takeaways from China's Battery Expansion?

China's commitment to adding 600+ GWh of battery production capacity represents a transformative development in global energy infrastructure. The strategic allocation of 70% toward energy storage systems rather than electric vehicle applications indicates recognition of grid-scale storage as the primary growth market.

When Will These New Facilities Begin Production?

Some manufacturing facilities are scheduled to begin production in late 2026, with full capacity ramp-up continuing into 2027 and beyond. The staggered timeline reflects the complexity of establishing large-scale battery manufacturing operations and obtaining necessary regulatory approvals.

Construction and commissioning of battery manufacturing facilities typically requires 12-24 months from groundbreaking to initial production, depending on facility size and technology complexity. Additional time is needed for production optimisation and quality certification processes.

The 19 manufacturers participating in the expansion will likely have different timelines based on their individual capacity requirements, technology choices, and site preparation status. Market impact will occur gradually as facilities come online rather than simultaneously.

How Will This Affect Global Battery Prices?

Increased production capacity generally creates downward pressure on battery prices through economies of scale and competitive pressures among manufacturers. The 900 GWh annual capacity represents substantial supply addition that could influence global pricing dynamics.

However, price impacts depend on demand growth rates and raw material costs, which could offset some manufacturing cost reductions. Strong demand growth from energy storage applications and continued EV adoption may absorb increased capacity without significant price declines.

Market segmentation between premium applications requiring advanced specifications and cost-sensitive applications accepting standard performance may create different pricing trajectories for various battery categories.

What Quality Standards Apply to Energy Storage Batteries?

Energy storage battery systems must comply with various international standards including IEC 62619 for safety requirements, UL 9540 for energy storage systems, and regional electrical codes governing grid-connected installations.

Quality standards for utility-scale applications typically require:

Cycle life testing demonstrating minimum performance over expected operational periods

Safety certifications covering thermal runaway prevention and fire suppression

Grid integration compliance including power quality and control system requirements

Environmental durability testing for outdoor installation conditions

Chinese manufacturers must achieve international certifications to access global markets, creating quality improvement incentives despite rapid capacity scaling pressures. Certification processes may influence production timelines and market entry strategies.

The scale and timing of China's battery manufacturing expansion will fundamentally reshape global energy storage markets. Furthermore, understanding these developments helps stakeholders navigate the evolving landscape of renewable energy integration and grid modernisation requirements. text:
Renovations Will Allow Center to Better Serve Teen Community in City’s Southwest Quadrant

NYS Investment Bolsters Continued Agency Workforce Development Programs Supporting the Region’s Comprehensive Strategy to Revitalize Communities and Grow the Economy

Empire State Development (ESD) marked the completion of a $560,000 upgrade to the Boys and Girls Club Teen Center in the City of Rochester. The updated Genesee Street facility will serve as the central hub for teen programming at the Club, providing a safe, supportive environment where young people can develop essential life skills, build confidence, and prepare for adulthood. The renovation will not only allow the center to better serve the teen community, but will also expand their workforce development component New Yorks State’s $112,000 investment in this important project, facilitated by a grant from the Finger Lakes Regional Economic Development Council (FLREDC), was first announced on site by Governor Kathy Hochul in March of 2023 during a stop at the center.

Empire State Development President, CEO and Commissioner Hope Knight said, “By investing in our communities, we are supporting the next generation of New Yorkers and ensuring that families can live, learn, and succeed together. This project will help the young people of Rochester secure meaningful opportunities for growth. Under Governor Hochul’s leadership, and thanks to the dedicated work of the statewide Regional Economic Development Council initiative, New York State continues to create safe spaces that are empowering children to flourish and thrive.”

The Teen Center updates included new floors, walls, computers, gaming equipment, the addition of a movie space, and room for implementing the program’s career exploration and job development programming. The project was additionally supported by local foundations and individual donors.

Founded in 1971 at the old Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT) campus in the Third Ward, the agency moved its headquarters to its current location at 500 Genesee Street in 1980 to better serve area youth. The organization offers over 30 quality youth development programs that are designed to develop character and develop life-enhancing skills.

“This Teen Center represents more than just a new space—it’s a commitment to our teens and their future,” said Dwayne Mahoney, Executive Director of the Boys & Girls Clubs of Rochester. “We are creating opportunities for young people to learn, grow, and succeed in a safe and supportive environment.”

The Finger Lakes Regional Economic Development Council (FLREDC) is a public-private partnership aimed at developing long-term strategic plans for economic growth in the nine-county Finger Lakes region. It focuses on creating jobs, driving private investment, empowering stakeholders, reducing poverty, supporting startup businesses and strengthening workforce development among other priorities.

Finger Lakes Regional Economic Development Co-Chairs Bob Duffy, President and CEO, Greater Rochester Chamber of Commerce and Monroe Community College President Dr. DeAnna Burt-Nanna said, “The FLREDC is dedicated to supporting the next generation, helping them to succeed. These impactful updates to the Boys and Girls Club’s Teen Center in Rochester will bolster those efforts, working to create significant opportunities for young people here, resulting in a brighter future for all of us.”

The Regional Economic Development Council initiative is a key component of the State's approach to State investment and economic development. In 2011, 10 Regional Councils were established to develop long-term strategic plans for economic growth for their regions. The Councils are public-private partnerships made up of local experts and stakeholders from business, academia, local government, and non-governmental organizations. The Regional Councils have redefined the way New York invests in jobs and economic growth by putting in place a community-based, bottom-up approach and establishing a competitive process for State resources.

State Senator Jeremy Cooney said, “The Boys & Girls Club Teen Center has bettered the lives of countless youth in our community, empowering those of all backgrounds to achieve their goals and build a better future. It’s only right that we support them in this mission, which is why I want to thank Governor Hochul and Empire State Development for their leadership on this project which will mean better outcomes and better resources to ensure the success of teens throughout our community.”

State Assemblymember Demond Meeks said, "Providing a safe and supportive haven for our teens is a top priority, and these renovations at the Boys and Girls Club Teen Center make that vision a reality for the Genesee Street community. This project represents a vital collaboration between the state and local partners to ensure our young people have access to high-quality resources right in their own neighborhood. With enhanced programming and modernized facilities, we are empowering our youth to build confidence and pursue their goals in a space designed specifically for their success. This $560,000 investment is a testament to our ongoing commitment to strengthening the social fabric of the Southwest Quadrant."

Monroe County Executive Adam Bello said, “Investing in our youth is an investment in the very future of Monroe County. These renovations to the Boys and Girls Club Teen Center will strengthen an already vital support system that has been a keystone of the area for over 40 years. The new space will expand opportunities, inspire growth, and empower our young people to thrive and succeed. Thank you to Governor Hochul and Empire State Development for delivering this critical funding and reaffirming their commitment to our community’s next generation.”

City of Rochester Mayor Malik D. Evans said, "The transformation of this space is a meaningful milestone for our community, and everyone served by the Boys and Girls Clubs of Rochester. Thanks to the generous commitment of Governor Hochul, New York State, local foundations and private supporters, the new Teen Center will be a cornerstone for learning, growth, and achievement for generations to come."

For additional information about the Rochester Boys and Girls Club, visit: https://bgcrochester.org/.

For additional information about the Regional Economic Development Council Initiative, visit: regionalcouncils.ny.gov.

Accelerating Economic Development in the Finger Lakes

Today’s announcement complements “Finger Lakes Forward,” the region’s comprehensive strategy to generate robust economic growth and community development. The regionally designed plan focuses on investing in key industries including photonics, agriculture‎ and food production, and advanced manufacturing. More information is available here.

About Empire State Development

Empire State Development is New York's chief economic development agency, and promotes business growth, job creation, and greater economic opportunity throughout the state. With offices in each of the state's 10 regions, ESD oversees the Regional Economic Development Councils, supports broadband equity through the ConnectALL office, and is growing the workforce of tomorrow through the Office of Strategic Workforce Development. The agency engages with emerging and next generation industries like clean energy and semiconductor manufacturing looking to grow in New York State, operates a network of assistance centers to help small businesses grow and succeed, and promotes the state's world class tourism destinations through I LOVE NY. For more information, please visit esd.ny.gov, and connect with ESD on LinkedIn, Facebook and X.

text:
On April 7, U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke L. Rollins announced the USDA has finalized a rule modernizing the National Environmental Policy Act regulations. This Final Rule adopts the changes introduced in the Interim Final Rule published on July 3, 2025, which consolidated seven agency-specific NEPA regulations into a single, department wide framework, reducing the overall volume of regulations by 66 percent. This major action is also a linchpin in Secretary Rollins’ broader Deregulatory Agenda for U.S. Agriculture and Consumers (PDF, 5.1 MB).

“Since last July, agencies at USDA have shown they can reduce environmental review timelines by up to 80%. These faster, more efficient reviews are saving the Department millions in taxpayer dollars,” said Secretary Rollins. “Those savings benefit the American people, and quicker reviews mean the loans, critical infrastructure, and forest health projects our farmers, ranchers, and rural communities depend on can move forward sooner. USDA is proud to help advance President Trump’s vision of a government that serves its citizens, beginning with cutting unnecessary bureaucratic overreach.”

“NEPA is a procedural statute meant to ensure the government considers reasonable environmental analysis before making a final decision,” said Deputy Secretary Vaden. “It has morphed into the greatest roadblock to everything from protecting our National Forests from devastating wildfires to constructing much needed roadways. With this reform, we return NEPA to its intended role of requiring analysis and unleash the ability of USDA to once again get the American people’s work done.”

For years, USDA agencies observed how overregulation turned the NEPA process into a form of bureaucratic overreach that hindered American innovation, eliminated jobs, and increased costs for Americans. The changes in the Final Rule restore USDA’s NEPA implementation to its core purpose: ensuring federal agencies consider environmental impacts while maintaining the flexibility needed for efficient permitting and faster delivery of critical USDA services and funding relied on by farmers, ranchers, loggers, and rural communities.

title: U.S. LNG Exports Soar To Record Levels In March Amid Panic Buying | OilPrice.com
description:
U.S. liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports hit a record 11.7 million metric tons in March 2026, mainly driven by global panic buying and supply disruptions triggered by geopolitical tensions in the Middle East.
Louisiana Plaquemines LNG plant has been contributing significantly to U.S. LNG output growth as it continues to ramp up production.
Other than the Plaquemines LNG megaproject, Louisiana is also home to Delfin LNG, a proposed deepwater port project in Louisiana.
Delfin LNG is slated to become the first U.S. floating liquefied natural gas (FLNG) export facility.
Delfin LNG is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Delfin Midstream Inc., a developer of FLNG vessels.
text:
U.S. liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports hit a record 11.7 million metric tons in March 2026, mainly driven by global panic buying and supply disruptions triggered by geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. Missile and drone attacks on Qatar's Ras Laffan Industrial City in March damaged critical infrastructure, forcing major outages and positioning the U.S. as a vital swing producer. LNG facilities in Louisiana handled roughly 1.8 million more metric tons in March 2026 compared to March 2025, with Louisiana currently handling ~61% of all U.S. LNG shipments. Europe remained the top destination, accounting for approximately 7.49 million tons, or 64%, of total U.S. exports of super-chilled gas. A substantial premium for international gas prices over the U.S. Henry Hub price also incentivized increased export activities, with European TTF and Asian LNG benchmarks trading at a massive premium to U.S. Henry Hub prices, which hovered around $3 per MMBtu. While Henry Hub prices were relatively stable due to strong production, the high international prices (TTF, JKM) ensured maximum utilization of U.S. export terminals, which were running near capacity.

Louisiana Plaquemines LNG plant has been contributing significantly to U.S. LNG output growth as it continues to ramp up production. The Venture Global LNG facility received immediate authorization from the Department of Energy for a 13% increase in exports, adding up to 0.45 billion cubic feet of natural gas per day to meet surging global demand. Plaquemines LNG is designed with an initial, fully contracted capacity of 20 million metric tonnes per annum (mpta). However, the facility has shown it can exceed its original nameplate capacity by up to 40% thanks to the high performance of its modular design.

Related: Saudi Arabia Sets Record Premium for Flagship Crude as Hormuz Crisis Deepens

The project is undergoing expansion, with long-term plans to exceed 45–58 mpta total capacity through additional modular trains to bring the total to 36 trains. Plaquemines LNG is one of the largest private infrastructure projects in the U.S., with total project costs estimated at nearly $24 billion when completed.

Other than the Plaquemines LNG megaproject, Louisiana is also home to Delfin LNG, a proposed deepwater port project in Louisiana. Delfin LNG is slated to become the first U.S. floating liquefied natural gas (FLNG) export facility. The project will support three FLNG vessels producing up to 13.2 mpta. Located ~30 miles off Cameron Parish in the southwest corner of Louisiana, Delfin LNG will repurpose the UTOS pipeline and connect it with the High Island Offshore Gas Pipeline (HIOS) to transport feedgas to the floating LNG vessels. By utilizing these existing offshore pipelines and constructing a new 700-foot bypass to connect them (the Delfin Offshore Pipeline), the project will minimize additional infrastructure investment, classifying it as a "brownfield" deepwater port project. A February 2026 pipeline explosion and associated regulatory hurdles have delayed the Final Investment Decision (FID), which is now anticipated in the spring of 2026. Delfin LNG is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Delfin Midstream Inc., a developer of FLNG vessels. The project is primarily backed by Fairwood Peninsula Energy Corp (approx. 30.7%), along with Talisman Global Alternative Master LP and Talisman Global Capital Master.

U.S. LNG exports are expected to rise by ~13% in 2026, driven by new capacity from Venture Global LNG's Plaquemines and Cheniere Energy's (NYSE:LNG) Corpus Christi Stage 3. Port Arthur LNG (Texas) and Rio Grande LNG are scheduled to begin operations between 2027-2028, with further projects expected to come online in 2030/2031.

The Permian Basin’s gas production is projected to rise, driven by increasing associated gas output, which will help meet surging demand from the U.S. Gulf Coast LNG export terminals. Permian natural gas production is expected to hit 28 Bcf/d in the current year, solidifying the basin’s role as the fastest-growing gas-producing play in the U.S. Permian wells are currently producing record amounts of associated residue natural gas at approximately 22 Bcf/d, which is expected to rise to ~28 Bcf/d in 2026, comprising roughly one-fifth of total U.S. production.

Overall, U.S. LNG export capacity is projected to more than double between 2024 and 2028, with exports expected to rise from 11.9 Bcf/d in 2024 to 21.5 Bcf/d by 2030, reinforcing the country’s position as the top global exporter. The rapid expansion requires significant new infrastructure to transport the feedgas. Thankfully, the startup of projects like the Matterhorn Express Pipeline is expected to mitigate takeaway capacity constraints, helping to stabilize Waha Hub prices.

title: Trump's 'Radical' Species Permitting Merger Carries Legal Risks - Bloomberg Law News
description:
The legal basis for the Trump administration’s proposed merger of endangered species permitting under a single office is unclear and could require Congress to amend the law, natural resources lawyers say.
The proposal calls for a $6 million cut to spending on listing species under the ESA and even deeper cuts to endangered species conservation and consultation programs.
The Trump administration has taken numerous steps over the last year to lift endangered species protections, including recently convening the Endangered Species Committee to exempt Gulf of Mexico oil operations from the ESA.
The Center for Biological Diversity is looking into whether the proposed merger has a sound legal basis, said Noah Greenwald, endangered species director at the Center, which has filed suit against the Endangered Species Committee.
“They’re not really concerned about Congressional authority.” The proposed budget now heads to Congress.
text:
The legal basis for the Trump administration’s proposed merger of endangered species permitting under a single office is unclear and could require Congress to amend the law, natural resources lawyers say.

And environmental groups say they worry the proposed consolidation of Endangered Species Act permitting will degrade the federal government’s ability to enforce the law and prevent the extinction of plants and animals.

“I can’t think of any other specific examples of where multiple agencies having overlapping jurisdiction have been merged into one agency,” said Larry Liebesman, a former Justice Department attorney who is a senior adviser for environmental permitting firm Dawson & Associates. “It’s a fairly radical approach.”

The White House’s fiscal 2027 budget request calls for endangered species permitting at the Commerce Department’s National Marine Fisheries Service and the US Fish and Wildlife Service to be consolidated into a single office at the Interior Department, which would issue permits for developers to harass or kill, known as “take,” imperiled marine and land wildlife.

Interior’s budget justification calls for all Commerce Department ESA programs to be consolidated under FWS, with a proposed new allocation of $178 million for marine species. The proposal calls for a $6 million cut to spending on listing species under the ESA and even deeper cuts to endangered species conservation and consultation programs.

“With this proposal, FWS would take over the workload of listing, delisting, and consulting on projects impacting endangered species and have sufficient funding to maintain marine mammal stock assessments,” the justification says.

The Trump administration has taken numerous steps over the last year to lift endangered species protections, including recently convening the Endangered Species Committee to exempt Gulf of Mexico oil operations from the ESA. That decision would possibly jeopardize the Rice’s whale, which NMFS found in 2025 could be driven to extinction by offshore oil drilling. The administration is also expected to soon finalize a rule that would allow an imperiled species’ habitat to be destroyed without it being considered harmful to the species.

The Endangered Species Act and a 1970 federal government reorganization plan require the Commerce secretary to oversee endangered and threatened marine species and the Interior Department’s US Fish and Wildlife Service to oversee species on land.

Consolidating marine and onshore ESA permitting into the Interior Department is necessary because permitting by separate agencies has “created unnecessary red tape, increased costs, delayed approvals, and produced inconsistent outcomes for permittees,” the budget request says.

But the law is explicit about the Secretary of Commerce having the authority to administer the ESA for species in its jurisdiction, said Rebecca Hays Barho, partner at Nossaman LLP in Austin.

“The proposed budget does not provide the legal mechanism by which NMFS’ duties could be re-assigned to USFWS, and it’s unclear whether this could be done absent action by Congress,” she said.

The Interior Department didn’t respond to a request for comment.

‘Radical’ Move

A merger could result in more efficient permitting, but it would likely be an unprecedented move, Liebesman said.

The merger would likely lead to weakened ESA enforcement, said Gary Rule, a former NMFS fisheries biologist in Oregon who worked on ESA permitting and took a voluntary early retirement offer last year.

“I suspect they’d probably delist a bunch of species, change of bunch of regulations, and simplify things quite a bit,” he said.

The merger was first proposed last year, and it was followed by numerous voluntary retirements and employee firings by the Trump administration, gutting NMFS offices responsible for ESA permitting, Rule said.

“Twenty to 30% of folks took it because it looked like they were going to eliminate that part of the agency and a lot of us would just be laid off,” he said.

The Center for Biological Diversity is looking into whether the proposed merger has a sound legal basis, said Noah Greenwald, endangered species director at the Center, which has filed suit against the Endangered Species Committee.

“I think this administration just in so many regards have shown they don’t care about the rule of law,” he said. “They’re not really concerned about Congressional authority.”

The proposed budget now heads to Congress. Lawmakers ignored most of the Interior Department budget cuts the Trump administration proposed for fiscal 2026, which included transferring some national parks to local governments or private entities.

text:
A close look at the Administration’s wreckage, in six steps

The second Trump Administration has brought a flood of obstacles to the national effort to transition away from petroleum-powered vehicles to electric vehicles (EVs). These challenges have come in many forms across multiple levels of government; they are in most cases completely unprecedented, and in many cases legally dubious (to put it mildly).

The push to electrify in the US was on precarious but improving footing before Trump took office. The recent legislative, regulatory, and litigation steps are destabilizing that push in all aspects. Fifteen months (and one illegal, maybe paused, oil shock-generating war) in, these actions are sufficiently numerous and interrelated that it can be hard to keep track of their origins and impacts.

The benefits of the transition (improved air quality and public health, reduced climate-warming emissions, lower long-term costs for drivers, independence from fossil fuels) and barriers to realizing it (upfront costs, charging limitations, battery supply constraints and mining justice concerns, domestic manufacturer hesitance, oil industry opposition) are well known and only bear repeating to illustrate the full scope of the Administration’s actions.

In the most simplified form, the Administration (and Congress) have done three primary things: 1) eliminate financial incentives for consumers to buy or lease an EV; 2) repeal federal standards requiring automakers to reduce vehicle emissions and sell more EVs; and 3) attack California’s special authority to separately require the same. (This list focuses on automobiles and does not highlight all the parallel measures taken to attack clean truck regulation, which is hugely important for air quality in underserved communities in particular; nor does it include the significant impacts of tariffs, proposed legislation to block new emissions regulations, or related attacks on clean energy development.)

1. Eliminating Incentives

In July 2025, Congress passed and President Trump signed a massive tax and spending bill that largely eliminated the electric vehicle (EV) incentive programs created by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). The IRA programs that were terminated include:

An up to $7,500 tax credit for new EV purchases

An up to $4,000 credit for used EV purchases

An up to $40,000 credit for commercial heavy-duty EV purchases that enabled incentives for leased automobiles as well

A credit for up to 30% of the cost for EV charger installations at eligible properties

The impacts of these actions are still unclear–EV sales enjoyed a bump last fall before the expiration date, followed by an expected sharp drop–but a significant sales slowdown is probably inevitable. Pulling billions of dollars out of the market is very likely to have the intended effect of cutting the appeal of EVs for drivers, which domestic manufacturers have anticipated by eliminating multiple existing and planned models.

2. Repealing Federal Standards

Endangerment finding rescission: In February, EPA formally rescinded the greenhouse gas (GHG) endangerment finding, which is the agency’s formal determination that GHGs emissions endanger human health and welfare and merit regulation under the Clean Air Act. Dozens of states and environmental groups have challenged the action, which stands on slim legal footing. If the courts allow the rescission to proceed, EPA would effectively (due to its own actions) be unable to regulate vehicle GHGs, in turn unwinding the basis for much federal zero-emission vehicle (and EV) regulation. More traditional regulatory authority addressing the criteria pollutant emissions of combustion engines (which you can thank for your catalytic converter) would not be affected unless EPA followed up with some fairly esoteric legal maneuvers. Many legal experts argue that rescinding the endangerment finding would, in fact, free states to enact their own GHG standards without federal preemption, since the federal government will no longer have standards in place. But EPA will likely claim that the Clean Air Act universally preempts state standards even for pollutants it (allegedly) does not cover.

Emissions standards rollback: In the same action, EPA also formally rescinded a host of federal GHG emissions standards for trucks and automobiles, claiming that the withdrawal of the endangerment finding eliminated the legal basis for those standards. Most prominently, those standards would have led to EVs constituting approximately 68% of new automobile sales nationwide by 2032. Legal challenges to the rescission are underway. If it is upheld, it will mean that there are no federal requirements to reduce auto and truck GHG emissions. While older standards governing the criteria pollutant emissions of combustion engines would remain in place, they would provide a very limited regulatory incentive for further manufacturer investments in EVs.

Fuel economy standards enforcement zero-out: In addition to repealing the IRA incentives for EVs, the 2025 tax and spending bill eliminated the penalties manufacturers have to pay for violations of the Corporate Average Fuel Economy requirements. (In the context of reducing vehicle GHG emissions, which cannot be scrubbed or filtered by engine modifications, fuel efficiency and emissions control are largely synonymous.) Setting noncompliance penalties to zero is effectively the same as repealing the standards, as Dan argued recently. This action has the same basic effect as the GHG emissions standards rollback, essentially eliminating federal regulatory drivers for manufacturers to produce EVs instead of fossil fuel vehicles.

3. Attacking California Authority:

Clean Air Act waiver nullification: In three related actions in mid-2025, Congress passed and President Trump signed resolutions under the Congressional Review Act that (purportedly) nullified waivers previously issued to allow California to enforce its own state-level vehicle emissions standards (for automobiles, embodied in the GHG emissions requirements and zero-emission vehicle sales requirements of the Advanced Clean Cars II program). The Clean Air Act bars states from regulating vehicle emissions, except when California proposes standards that meet specific requirements and the Environmental Protection Agency grants a preemption waiver. The Congressional Review Act allows Congress and the President to overturn certain agency regulations issued at the end of a prior administration and bars agencies from issuing substantially similar rules in the future. (It should not apply at all to administrative approvals like waiver actions, an issue which is currently being litigated.) If these actions survive judicial review, then California would not be able to enforce its landmark targets of 100% zero-emission automobile sales by 2035 and truck sales by 2045, and arguably could be prevented from proposing similar targets under a more favorable future administration.

California standards preemption challenge: In March, the Administration sued California to block enforcement of the state’s Advanced Clean Cars I standards, a set of GHG emissions and ZEV sales requirements that preceded ACC II. After Congress (purportedly) nullified the waiver for ACC II, CARB issued an emergency regulation reinstating ACC I on the basis that the waiver issued by EPA in 2013 was still in effect. The Administration argues that the ACC I standards are preempted because the federal Energy Policy and Conservation Act prevents states from enacting their own fuel economy standards for vehicles, and the GHG emissions standards and ZEV sales requirements are “related to fuel economy standards” because they have the effect of reducing average fuel consumption statewide. If the litigation succeeds, California could be barred from enforcing even its last set of clean vehicle regulations, which combined with the federal standards rollback would largely pause existing US regulatory efforts seeking to advance the EV transition.

With so many legally dubious moves in litigation, it is impossible to ascertain the net effect on the EV transition at this point. A successful repeal of the GHG endangerment finding could open up the playing field to state-level vehicle regulations like ACC II. A convoluted set of federal court rulings could approve of the Administration’s exit from the regulatory field while still finding that the federal emissions and fuel economy laws preempt state action. A new administration in 2029 could reverse the rules and withdraw the lawsuits, but even resetting to the 2024-era status quo could take years.

In the meantime, the additional pollution from gasoline and diesel will continue to cause thousands of avoidable cases of asthma and cancer, increase the severity of climate catastrophe, and expose us to the risks of the international oil markets. And those of us who would like to avert these unnecessary harms are increasingly left to look for alternative pathways.

text:
ProPublica and The Texas Tribune have selected five new partner organizations in Texas to participate in the second year of a local investigative initiative that supports accountability journalism in newsrooms across the state.

Over the next year, the five newsrooms — Big Bend Sentinel, the Houston Chronicle, KRIS 6 News in Corpus Christi, KXAN Investigates in Austin and the Texas Observer — will report on state and federal efforts to restrict local control, in collaboration with the Texas investigative unit housed at ProPublica and the Tribune.

In the first year of the program, state partners published deep dives into a controversial campaign to overhaul Dallas city government and the growing political power of a North Texas church called Mercy Culture; examined one of the state’s most influential lobbying groups; broke down El Paso’s struggles to build its aerospace industry; and explored Elon Musk’s increasing sway over state government. Two partners, The Texas Newsroom and the Houston Chronicle, collaborated to reveal efforts by Musk’s The Boring Company to build a flood tunnel in Houston with the help of an area congressman.

“The first year of our Texas investigative initiative demonstrated the critical role local newsrooms play in holding accountable the powerful officials of this very influential state. We are eager to keep working with local partners, so together we can be force multipliers and produce strong investigative journalism,” said Vianna Davila, deputy editor of the ProPublica-Tribune investigative unit.

The ProPublica-Tribune investigative unit started in 2020, when the newsrooms launched a first-of-its-kind collaboration to produce investigative reporting for and about Texas. Both organizations publish the team’s stories, which are distributed for free to other news outlets in Texas and beyond.

Big Bend Sentinel

Big Bend Sentinel is a weekly nonprofit print publication, with daily online stories, covering Far West Texas. The Big Bend spans three counties: Presidio, Brewster and Jeff Davis — a mountainous high desert area about the size of Switzerland.

Based in Marfa, Big Bend Sentinel focuses on in-depth reporting of local news, people and the arts in Marfa, Presidio, Alpine, Terlingua, Fort Davis, other Big Bend communities and Ojinaga, Mexico. Spanish-language stories are included each week to meet the needs of readers who prefer their news in their native language.

The news organization has emerged as a leading source of information on the federal government’s plan to build a border wall along the Rio Grande in the Big Bend region.

Houston Chronicle

The Houston Chronicle is the largest newsroom in Texas, covering the nation’s fourth-largest city. It has won the Pulitzer Prize three times.

Recent investigations have spurred reforms to utility practices at CenterPoint, the region’s energy provider; prompted the governor to call for an investigation into a $95 million Texas Lottery jackpot scheme; and exposed the risks of “zombie” oil and gas wells that can spread toxic wastewater. As part of the Chronicle’s coverage of July 4 floods that killed more than 130 people, it revealed that local officials chose to cut property taxes rather than modernize a flood warning system and that buildings were removed from the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s flood maps, including some in the camp where 27 girls and their counselors died. Legislators later passed laws requiring camp safety plans and limiting development in floodplains, and local officials pledged $1.5 million for an enhanced warning system.

KRIS 6 News

KRIS 6 News in Corpus Christi has served South Texas as the Coastal Bend’s NBC affiliate since 1956. The newsroom was recognized for Overall Texas Broadcast Excellence at the 2025 Texas Broadcast News Awards and has won multiple awards for public records reporting.

In its “Facing Danger” series, the newsroom exposed design flaws in the ramps to the Harbor Bridge that contributed to eight deaths in seven years from wrong-way drivers. It also uncovered $350 million in potentially illegal workforce housing deals with the Corpus Christi Housing Authority, revealed problems inside the Nueces County medical examiner’s office and uncovered lavish public spending by the Port of Corpus Christi’s executive director. Since August, KRIS 6 has been covering Corpus Christi’s intensifying water crisis through its “Running Dry” series.

KXAN Investigates

KXAN Investigates is a team of Austin-based journalists who tackle stories that spark policy change, hold leaders accountable and make communities safer. Its investigative work has received many honors, including seven national Edward R. Murrow Awards.

In 2019, KXAN Investigates launched the station’s digital-first unit, “Catalyst,” which uses innovative storytelling methods to investigate complex topics like flaws in the state’s missing persons system, mental competency challenges among Texas inmates and people dying in police custody. Since early 2025, the team has also led a larger group of 20 journalists in a multiplatform crowdsourcing project called “Undocumented: Texas’ Immigration Impact in a New Trump Era,” which explores the community impact of a new presidential administration’s aggressive approach to immigration enforcement.

Texas Observer

The Texas Observer is a nonprofit news outlet and print magazine that strives to make Texas a more equitable place through investigative reporting, narrative storytelling, and political and cultural coverage. Since its founding in 1954, the Observer has focused on communities whose stories are too often ignored or poorly told. It seeks not only to inform but to empower its readers, as it works to hold public officials and corporations accountable.

title: Climate change doesn't care about your bandwidth | News From The States
description:
Some commentators have suggested that no one has the bandwidth anymore to think about climate change.
But climate change doesn’t care about your bandwidth, and conditions in Colorado prove the point.
There is no scientific doubt that climate change contributes to bigger, fiercer wildfires and other extreme ecological events, and there is no scientific doubt that the primary cause of climate change is the human combustion of fossil fuels.
But, though it usually doesn’t produce spectacular daily headlines, climate change threatens eventually to leave whole regions of the Earth uninhabitable.
The worst effects of climate change can still be avoided, but only if voters insist leaders address it with the emergency response it demands.
text:
So many crises threaten society these days. Daily news about war, the emergence of AI, runaway costs of living, the threat of new pandemics, the growing dangers of fascism in Washington — it’s a deluge of worry, and it can be hard to think about much else.

But the pile of troubles in recent years has diverted attention from the long-term crisis of climate change, arguably humanity’s supreme challenge, which is not going away just because it gets less attention. Some commentators have suggested that no one has the bandwidth anymore to think about climate change. But climate change doesn’t care about your bandwidth, and conditions in Colorado prove the point.

The state just had its warmest winter on record by almost 2 degrees Fahrenheit, and average temperatures from December through February were more than 8 degrees above the 20th century average, as Newsline reported last month. Cities up and down the Front Range saw record-high numbers of 60-degree days this winter. The state is also fantastically dry, part of an aridification process driven by global warming.

As reporter Chase Woodruff wrote, “Hotter, drier conditions in Colorado have stressed water supplies, made the state’s forests more vulnerable to insects and diseases, and greatly increased wildfire risk.”

Waterways in Colorado this year are universally expected to see below-normal flows, including the Colorado River, which is forecast to run at just 68% of normal. The Colorado River, a vital resource for 40 million people, this century has experienced critical streamflow depletions. The river is down 20% from historic annual averages. Some projections suggest Lake Powell, a crucial reservoir on the river, could drop for the first time below the minimum level needed for it to produce hydropower at the Glen Canyon Dam, energy generation relied on by almost 6 million people.

Low snowpack that’s contributing to streamflow shortages is also a blow to the Colorado ski industry, which generates $4.8 billion a year and supports more than 46,000 jobs across the state. At the current trajectory, the industry will disappear by the end of the century. Climate modeling shows the ski season could be shortened by more than a month by 2050 and more than two months by 2090. And it’s not just less snow — climate change is to blame for increasingly poor snow.

The latest forecasts suggest Coloradans should brace for more brutal wildfires this year. Hot and dry conditions, along with low moisture content in vegetative fuels, are already at levels on the Front Range typical of peak fire season. Worsening conditions as summer unfolds will further increase the state’s vulnerability to wildfires. Tinderbox conditions are becoming the norm: The three largest wildfires in Colorado history all occurred in 2020, and the state’s 20 biggest fires have all occurred in the past 20 years.

There is no scientific doubt that climate change contributes to bigger, fiercer wildfires and other extreme ecological events, and there is no scientific doubt that the primary cause of climate change is the human combustion of fossil fuels.

Yet government policies, especially as guided by MAGA priorities, reject the science. In February, the Trump administration revoked the so-called endangerment finding, which recognized the dangers of greenhouse gas emissions and allowed climate regulations under the Clean Air Act. The administration is forcing coal-fired power generation in Colorado to persist past a planned retirement date, apparently to accommodate coal business interests.

Climate change so far has not figured prominently in 2026 statewide elections. The platforms of the top Democratic candidates for governor, U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet and Attorney General Phil Weiser, both mention climate change as a problem to confront. But Bennet touts a “market-based path to cut emissions” that resembles the disappointing carrot-over-stick approach of the administration of Gov. Jared Polis, under whom the state has failed to meet its own greenhouse gas emission reduction targets.

Many Coloradans fear the federal government, and they’re struggling to pay for housing, health care and other necessities, while national and world events seem ever more alarming. But, though it usually doesn’t produce spectacular daily headlines, climate change threatens eventually to leave whole regions of the Earth uninhabitable.

The worst effects of climate change can still be avoided, but only if voters insist leaders address it with the emergency response it demands.

CANDIAC — Claude Guay, Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources — accompanied by Member of Parliament Jacques Ramsay — announced over $11 million in funding for three projects under Natural Resources Canada’s Energy Innovation Program (EIP) – Battery Industry Acceleration Call for Proposals. These investments are meant to support innovation in battery materials and help strengthen Canada’s growing battery and critical minerals value chain, especially in Quebec, according to the federal government in a press release.

The funding will reportedly support projects led by Nano One Materials Corp., EcoPro Lithium Inc. and NanoXplore.

Nano One Materials Corp.’s Commercialization of Nano One’s One-Pot Process for Lithium Iron Phosphate Production project will receive $4.3 million to improve and scale up the production of lithium iron phosphate, a key battery material used in many lithium-ion batteries, including those used in electric vehicles and energy storage systems. This investment builds on a $5-million contribution under the EIP that was announced in 2025 to support Nano One’s work at its Candiac facility.

EcoPro Lithium Inc.’s Scale Up of the Process to Produce Battery-Grade Lithium Metal and Ultra-thin Lithium Anode Foil for Lithium Metal Batteries project will receive $6 million to scale up a new process to produce battery-grade lithium metal and ultra-thin lithium foil used in next-generation batteries. These materials will try to help batteries store more energy and reduce costs, supporting the development of more affordable electric vehicles.

NanoXplore’s Made-in-Canada Ultra-High-Power Li-ion 21700 Cylindrical Battery Cells project will receive nearly $700,000 for the prototyping of ultra-high-power-capacity lithium-ion cells. Building on a $2.75-million contribution under the EIP that was announced in 2025, this investment will try to strengthen domestic battery manufacturing for defence and civilian applications and reduce reliance on foreign suppliers.

“Quebec is an essential centre for battery innovation and advanced manufacturing. Projects like these help move new technologies closer to commercialization while reinforcing the province’s role in Canada’s growing clean technology sector. This is just one example of how Quebec is supporting our country to become a clean energy superpower,” said Claude Guay, Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources.

“NRCan supporting Nano One’s scale-up and automation in Candiac, as well as the development of future large plants, helps our company and in turn establishes a localized battery ecosystem. We strive to help Canada supply battery materials for critical applications domestically and for our allies in the short term and to become a reliable technology provider, based on homegrown IP, to help power and decarbonize transportation, energy grids and defence sectors globally,” said Adam Johnson, Senior Vice President, External Affairs, Nano One.

description:
